The answer is **yes**: $m(\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^{2n}: x-y\in E\})=0$.

**Proof.** Define the linear change of variables on $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ by
$$u = x - y, \qquad v = y,$$
so that $x = u+v$ and $y = v$. The map $\Phi:(u,v)\mapsto (x,y)=(u+v,\,v)$ is linear with block matrix
$$\begin{pmatrix} I_n & I_n \\ 0 & I_n \end{pmatrix},$$
whose determinant is $1$. Hence $\Phi$ is a Lebesgue-measure-preserving bijection of $\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ onto itself.

Under this change of variables the set in question becomes
$$S = \{(x,y): x-y\in E\} = \Phi\bigl(\{(u,v): u\in E\bigr)\bigr) = \Phi(E\times \mathbb{R}^n).$$
Since $\Phi$ preserves measure,
$$m_{2n}(S) = m_{2n}(E\times \mathbb{R}^n).$$

Now compute $m_{2n}(E\times\mathbb{R}^n)$ by Tonelli's theorem. Writing the indicator of $E\times\mathbb{R}^n$ as $\mathbf{1}_E(u)\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(v)$,
$$m_{2n}(E\times\mathbb{R}^n) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{2n}} \mathbf{1}_E(u)\,\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(v)\,du\,dv = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\mathbf{1}_E(u)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}dv\right)du = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\mathbf{1}_E(u)\cdot\infty\,du.$$

The integrand $g(u) = \mathbf{1}_E(u)\cdot\infty$ equals $\infty$ on $E$ and $0$ on $\mathbb{R}^n\setminus E$. Since $m(E)=0$, we have $g = 0$ almost everywhere. A nonnegative measurable function that vanishes a.e. has integral $0$, even if it takes the value $+\infty$ on a null set (the integral is the supremum of integrals of simple functions dominated by $g$, and every such simple function is supported in $E$ up to a null set, hence has integral $0$). Therefore
$$m_{2n}(E\times\mathbb{R}^n) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} g(u)\,du = 0.$$

Consequently $m_{2n}(S) = 0$, as claimed. $\blacksquare$
